examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix
examples.problem:
Let $J_n\left(\lambda\right)$ denote the $n \times n$ Jordan block matrix with $\lambda$ on the main diagonal. Then,  find
$e^{2\left(J_2(1) {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} J_2(3)\right)}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block $J_n(\lambda),$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/11519fece8adb61a999a33d66d9d61e3052709066702f96b8141a4574a8d86b8.png)

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2({J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))} & ={e}^{2([\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(1) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(3)\end{aligned}])} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2({J}_{2}(1))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{2({J}_{2}(3))}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{2({J}_{2}(1))}\,⊕\,{e}^{2({J}_{2}(3))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For $J_2(1),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=1.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2\cdot 1} & 2{e}^{2\cdot 1} \\ 0 & {e}^{2\cdot 1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & 2{e}^{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For $J_2(3),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=3.$ Since $n=2,$ we need the first derivative of $f$ only, which we have already computed. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2\cdot 3} & 2{e}^{2\cdot 3} \\ 0 & {e}^{2\cdot 3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6} & 2{e}^{6} \\ 0 & {e}^{6}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

feedback.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | $6$ | {{field-1}} | $-3$ | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{sin}⁡({J}_{4}(\frac{\pi }{6}))=\frac{1}{12}\,\,$ |  | $0$ | $6$ | {{field-3}} | $-3$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ |  |
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{4}(\frac{\pi }{6})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{6}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{6}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{6}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{6})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & -\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}6 & 6\sqrt{3} & -3 & -\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 6 & 6\sqrt{3} & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 6\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
